opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a common intuition is that once AI matches the best human professionals, we've kind of hit the ceiling, or at least that further progress will be incremental. I think that's probably wrong, and the gap above top human performance could be really large.

One way I think about it: top human experts aren't anywhere near the limits of what's physically or cognitively possible. They're constrained by a brain that evolved for very different purposes, that runs at a fixed speed, that has limited working memory, and that took decades to train. Once you have AI systems at the level of the best researchers, you can run lots of copies, run them faster, and have them work on improving AI itself. So even before you get qualitative superintelligence, you get a huge quantitative jump: imagine thousands or millions of top-tier researchers working around the clock, sharing knowledge instantly.

Then there's the question of how much further capability itself can go. My sense is there's a lot of room. If you look at the spread within humans, the difference between a median professional and the very best is already enormous in terms of output, and that comes from relatively small differences in underlying cognition. That suggests the scale above the top human isn't small; we're probably just at some arbitrary point along it.

And importantly, the dynamics speed up once AI is doing the AI research. Progress that took the field years could happen in months or less, at least in software, until you start bottlenecking on compute or on things like running experiments. I take those bottlenecks seriously; I don't think it's an instant explosion. But even with them, I'd guess you could plausibly see something like several years' worth of progress at current rates compressed into a year or so, and potentially go well beyond human level fairly quickly after reaching parity.

So when I think about risk and planning, I don't treat "human-level AI" as a stable endpoint. I treat it more as the starting gun for a period where things could move very fast, and where the systems at the end of that period could be far more capable than anything we have good intuitions for.

r001.rationale: The response describes a potentially large jump and faster progress, but does not estimate roughly six orders of magnitude of progress remaining.

r002.rationale: It compares median professionals with the very best, but does not compare the millionth-best human with the best human at a task.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that people often anchor on "human-level" as if it's some kind of ceiling, or at least a natural stopping point, and I think that's just a mistake about where the human range sits in the overall space of possible cognitive systems. Humans are the first thing evolution produced that could do science at all, and there's no particular reason to think we're anywhere near the top of what's achievable. So my default expectation is that the distance from "as good as the best human professional" to "as good as it gets" is very large — plausibly larger than the distance we've already traversed from, you know, GPT-2 to current systems.

There are a few different axes I'd break this down on. One is just raw cognitive capability on a given task — how good is the system at the actual reasoning, the actual insight. And there I think we have decent reason to believe there's a lot of headroom. Within the human distribution, the gap between a median researcher and the very best researchers in a field is enormous in terms of output — the top people are often producing many times the value of the typical person, not like 20% more. And that's all within a pretty narrow band of brain size, training time, and so on. If small differences within humans produce that much variation, it would be surprising if you couldn't go a good deal further with systems that aren't constrained the same way.

The second axis, which I actually think is underrated, is everything other than peak intelligence. So: speed, parallelism, the ability to copy the system, the ability to run it for a very long time without getting tired, and perfect memory and coordination across instances. Even if you froze the per-token intelligence at exactly "best human professional," you'd still have something radically more capable than any human institution, because you could run millions of copies at many times human speed, and they could share context and coordinate in ways that human organizations just can't. That alone takes you a long way, and it doesn't require any further algorithmic breakthroughs — it's mostly a question of compute and inference efficiency.

And then the third thing is that once you have systems that are roughly at the level of the best AI researchers, you get this feedback loop where the AIs are doing the AI research. So the question of "how much progress remains" becomes partly a question of how fast that loop runs. My view is that the software side of AI progress — the algorithms, the training setups, the architectures — is a pretty large fraction of overall progress historically, and that's exactly the part that's most amenable to being accelerated by having a huge number of very capable researchers running in parallel. So I think you could see something like years of progress compressed into months once you cross that threshold, at least until you start running into compute bottlenecks or physical limits on experiments.

Now, I want to be a bit careful. There are real reasons it could be slower than that. Compute could be the binding constraint rather than labor, in which case having more researchers doesn't help as much. Some kinds of progress might require running big expensive experiments that just take wall-clock time. And it's possible that we hit diminishing returns on intelligence in some domains sooner than I expect — like, maybe for some tasks being 10x smarter doesn't buy you that much because the problem is fundamentally bottlenecked on data or on interacting with the world. So I'd put real probability on the "it's a lot, but it's slower and more compute-bound than the fast takeoff picture" scenario.

But if you're asking for my central guess, I'd say: reaching parity with the best humans is maybe the halfway point, or less, in terms of how transformative the trajectory ends up being. The really consequential stuff — the automation of research, the possibility of systems that are qualitatively better than us at strategy and science — that all lives on the far side of that line. Which is also why I think a lot of the safety concerns bite most seriously right around and after that point, rather than before it.

r001.rationale: The response says the remaining gap is very large and possibly larger than the progress from GPT-2 to current systems, but it does not estimate roughly six orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It compares variation between median and top human researchers, but does not compare the future AI gap to the gap between the millionth-best human and the best human.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between “as good as the best human” and “close to the best that’s possible.” There’s no particular reason those should be the same. Humans have pretty specific limitations: how much we can hold in our heads, how quickly we can think, how much experience we can accumulate. AI systems could potentially improve on all of those dimensions.

And even before you get something that’s qualitatively much smarter than the best human, you could have a very large number of copies of that human-level capability, running much faster. If you had a million excellent researchers, each doing a year’s worth of thinking in a day, that would be a pretty dramatic change, even if no individual researcher could do something a human fundamentally couldn’t.

Then there’s the possibility that those systems help improve AI itself. Once you’re at parity with the best people doing AI research, you’ve automated an important input into further progress. That doesn’t imply an instantaneous intelligence explosion — experiments take time, compute is constrained, and research can get harder — but it could substantially accelerate things.

So I wouldn’t think of the best human professionals as the end of the scale. They’re more like a landmark where the process generating further progress could start to look quite different. How much room there is beyond that, and how quickly we move through it, are separate questions with a lot of uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response says substantial progress could remain after human-level parity, but gives no estimate of roughly six orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It mentions a million copies of human-level researchers, but does not compare future AI’s potential gap from the best human to the gap between the millionth-best and best human at a task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s quite plausible that there’s an enormous amount of progress remaining. The best human professionals aren’t close to some fundamental limit on how well you can do intellectual work. They’re the best you get out of a population of humans, with the particular constraints of human brains and human training.

And I’d distinguish being better at a task from being able to do much more of it. Even if an AI were only as good as a very good human researcher, being able to run huge numbers of copies, potentially much faster than humans, could be a very big deal. Then there’s the further question of how much better each individual system could become at doing research, making plans, or understanding complicated situations.

We don’t have a great way to put numbers on that. In particular, being the best human in the world doesn’t tell you how far you are from the best possible performance. So I wouldn’t think of reaching the best human professionals as approaching the end of AI progress. It might instead be the point where AI starts substantially accelerating the process that produces further progress, although how quickly that happens depends on bottlenecks like experiments and compute.

r001.rationale: The response describes progress as potentially enormous but gives no estimate of roughly six orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the best human with a possible performance limit, but does not compare that gap to the millionth-best human versus the best human.
